title: TANGCO: Learning Topology-Aware Capacity Allocation for Overload-driven Cascading Failures

paper.title: TANGCO : Learning Topology-Aware Capacity Allocation for Overload-driven Cascading Failures
paper.abstract:
Abstract. Many networked systems, from power grids to traffic networks and cloud clusters, carry loads across nodes with limited capacity.
A node whose load exceeds its capacity fails and sheds its load onto its neighbors, which can trigger a system-wide cascade.
We study how to allocate a fixed capacity budget across nodes to resist these cascades under local load redistribution.
The problem is difficult because no optimal allocation is known, and the fail-or-survive objective is non-differentiable and piecewise constant, so exact and gradient-based optimization methods do not directly apply.
We introduce TANGCO (Topology-Aware Neural Graph-Guided Capacity Optimization), which uses a graph neural network policy trained through the cascade simulator with policy-gradient learning and a heuristic anchor.
We evaluate TANGCO on five synthetic graph families and five real networks spanning power, road, air, and Internet topologies.
The learned policy improves on the best of four hand-designed heuristics in all 450 synthetic instances and in 40 of 45 real-network conditions, with robustness gains ranging from 1.6% to 246%.
The learned policies transfer to unseen graphs within a family and partially across related topologies, and TANGCO pre , pre-trained on synthetic graphs, matches per-network training on unseen real networks.
Training scales near-linearly with graph size, and TANGCO pre allocates on a new network with no per-target training, matching the deployment cost of a hand-designed heuristic.
Free-vector variants without the GNN, trained by policy gradient or by CMA-ES, stay close to the heuristics, so the graph representation carries the gain beyond numerical search; the depth analysis shows most of it arises from one-hop information.
Finally, analysis of the learned allocations identifies when local risk is sufficient, leads to an improved closed-form heuristic, and reveals the regimes where a topology-aware learned policy remains necessary.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Modern online services run on clusters of servers that share a request load. When one server becomes overloaded, its share of the load shifts to the remaining servers; if their updated load with the addition exceeds their capacity, they fail in turn, triggering a cascade that can end in a system-wide collapse. Such overload-driven cascades are a well-documented cause of large-scale outages at major cloud providers ( Bronson et al., 2021 ) . The same pattern is prevalent across many networked systems, including power grids ( Andersson et al., 2005 ) , transportation and traffic networks ( Li et al., 2015 ; Ma et al., 2020 ) , supply chains ( Yang et al., 2021 ; Hao et al., 2023 ) , as well as financial systems where the failure of one institution imposes losses on its counterparties and can push them into failure ( Gai and Kapadia, 2010 ) . In each case a node carries a load and fails when that load exceeds its capacity, and a failed node passes its load to other functioning nodes. The failure of a few components can therefore propagate through the network and bring down the system ( Buldyrev et al., 2010 ) . Cascading failures are due to network effects, where entities are connected through dependencies in a graph. The interaction between the graph topology and the capacity allocation of nodes therefore becomes critical in the cascade dynamics. Flow-based models of cascading failure originate with Motter and Lai ( Motter and Lai, 2002 ) , who take each node’s load to be its betweenness centrality and set its capacity to a fixed multiple of that load, c = ( 1 + α ) ​ l c=(1+\alpha)l . A large literature builds on this model to relate network structure to robustness and to add mechanisms such as dynamical recovery of failed nodes ( Majdandžić et al., 2014 ) and heterogeneous rules for how a failed node’s load spreads to its neighbors ( Hou et al., 2017 ) . Almost all work in this line fixes the allocated capacity in advance and studies the robustness that results ( Motter and Lai, 2002 ; Wang and Kim, 2007 ; Li et al., 2008 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) . The capacity allocation is thus an input to the model rather than a quantity to be designed. In this work, we treat capacity as a decision variable and address the problem of allocating a limited capacity budget across nodes to maximize robustness against cascading failures, a question that has received far less attention. The few works that study this allocation problem ( Zhang and Yağan, 2016 ; Ozel et al., 2018 ; Irsoy and Yagan, 2026a ) solve it under a global redistribution rule, where a failed node’s load is shared equally among all surviving nodes, irrespective of graph topology. That assumption yields a closed-form characterization of the final system size, and its allocations carry optimality guarantees while treating the network as fully connected and discarding topology. Under local redistribution, where loads pass only to immediate neighbors, cascade outcomes depend jointly on the topology and the initial load and capacity, and the global-redistribution guarantees no longer apply. Existing allocations for local redistribution are hand-designed heuristics rather than optimized methods. Hence, even though prior work has studied robustness extensively by analyzing and modifying network structure, the design question of how to allocate capacities on a given network and load remains far less explored. In contrast, we ask how to allocate a fixed capacity budget over a given network under local redistribution, where no optimal allocation is known. We introduce TANGCO (Topology-Aware Neural Graph-Guided Capacity Optimization), which employs a graph neural network (GNN) to learn capacity allocations directly from cascade dynamics. Given a graph and its initial loads, TANGCO outputs a capacity allocation that satisfies a fixed capacity budget. Our paper introduces four main contributions: • Topology-aware capacity optimization: We cast capacity allocation as a topology-aware policy-learning problem and propose TANGCO to maximize robustness against cascading failures. Hard overload thresholds make the cascade objective piecewise-constant; TANGCO trains a GNN allocation policy from simulator AUC rewards with score-function updates, without differentiating through the discrete failures. • Synthetic Pre-training and Transfer: We also introduce TANGCO pre , pretrained on diverse synthetic graph topologies and load distributions, and demonstrate strong transfer to unseen real-world networks (Figure 1 ). • Effectiveness, Scalability, Speed: Across five graph families, three load distributions, three capacity budgets, and five real-world networks, TANGCO consistently outperforms four competitive heuristics. Training scales linearly with graph size, while TANGCO pre needs no per-target training, yielding the best latency–performance trade-off (Figure 1 ). • Characterizing Gains: We show that message passing contributes consistently beyond direct numerical optimization, develop a one-hop rule that recovers most gains in specific regimes, and find that TANGCO ’s gains are largest on heterogeneous topologies at intermediate capacity budgets. sections.heading: 2. Problem Formulation
sections.text: We study overload-based cascading failures on an undirected graph G = ( 𝒱 , ℰ ) G=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}) with N = | 𝒱 | N=|\mathcal{V}| nodes. Each node v ∈ 𝒱 v\in\mathcal{V} has an initial load ℓ v \ell_{v} and a capacity c v c_{v} . The capacity is the maximum load that the node can carry before it fails. We write 𝐥 = ( ℓ v ) v ∈ 𝒱 \mathbf{l}=(\ell_{v})_{v\in\mathcal{V}} and 𝐜 = ( c v ) v ∈ 𝒱 \mathbf{c}=(c_{v})_{v\in\mathcal{V}} for the load and capacity vectors.

The cascade starts by removing the nodes in ℱ 0 \mathcal{F}_{0} . The loads of these nodes are then redistributed to the remaining network. After this redistribution, the surviving nodes are checked for overload. The same procedure is repeated in discrete iterations t = 1 , 2 , … t=1,2,\dots until no new node fails. Let ℓ v ( t ) \ell_{v}^{(t)} denote the load carried by node v v at iteration t t . The capacity c v c_{v} is fixed during the cascade. A node remains active at iteration t t if its current load does not exceed its capacity, i.e., ℓ v ( t ) ≤ c v \ell_{v}^{(t)}\leq c_{v} . If this condition is violated, the node fails and releases its current load for redistribution. sections.heading: 2.2. Capacity Allocation Problem
sections.text: The cascade model above determines the survival outcome for any fixed capacity assignment. Next, we consider how to allocate a given total capacity budget across the nodes of a given input graph to maximize robustness. This requires defining the feasible set of allocations and aggregating the robustness metric across failure sizes into a single objective.

sections.heading: 2.2.1. Capacity Constraint
sections.text: Because additional capacity is costly in practice, we fix a total capacity budget and treat the node capacities as the decision variables. With an unlimited budget, robustness is trivially maximized. We parameterize a node v v ’s capacity as (3) c v = ℓ v + s v , c_{v}=\ell_{v}+s_{v}, where s v ≥ 0 s_{v}\geq 0 is the excess capacity, or free space, assigned to node v v before any initial failures. This parameterization rules out trivial initial failures and simplifies the notation. Rather than optimize over capacities subject to ℓ v ≤ c v \ell_{v}\leq c_{v} , we optimize over non-negative free space under a fixed budget on the total free space. Let 𝐬 = ( s v ) v ∈ 𝒱 \mathbf{s}=(s_{v})_{v\in\mathcal{V}} denote the free-space vector. For a given free-space budget B B , the feasible allocations are (4) Δ B = { 𝐬 ∈ ℝ + N : ∑ v ∈ 𝒱 s v = B } . \Delta_{B}=\left\{\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{N}:\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}s_{v}=B\right\}. Thus, optimizing the capacity vector 𝐜 \mathbf{c} is equivalent to choosing a free-space allocation 𝐬 ∈ Δ B \mathbf{s}\in\Delta_{B} , with capacities given by c v = ℓ v + s v c_{v}=\ell_{v}+s_{v} . Given G G , 𝐥 \mathbf{l} , 𝐬 \mathbf{s} , and an initial failure set ℱ 0 \mathcal{F}_{0} , we write the final survival fraction as Φ ⁡ ( G , 𝐥 , 𝐬 , ℱ 0 ) \Phi(G,\mathbf{l},\mathbf{s};\mathcal{F}_{0}) .

sections.heading: 2.2.2. Robustness Objective
sections.text: The fraction Φ ⁡ ( G , 𝐥 , 𝐬 , ℱ 0 ) \Phi(G,\mathbf{l},\mathbf{s};\mathcal{F}_{0}) measures robustness against one fixed initial failure set, ℱ 0 \mathcal{F}_{0} . To evaluate an allocation for failures of a given size, let (5) 𝔽 k = { ℱ 0 ⊆ 𝒱 : | ℱ 0 | = k } \mathbb{F}_{k}=\left\{\mathcal{F}_{0}\subseteq\mathcal{V}:|\mathcal{F}_{0}|=k\right\} be the collection of all initial failure sets containing exactly k k nodes. The exact average survival fraction under k k initial failures is (6) J k ​ ( G , 𝐥 , 𝐬 ) = 1 ( N k ) ​ ∑ ℱ 0 ∈ 𝔽 k Φ ⁡ ( G , 𝐥 , 𝐬 , ℱ 0 ) . J_{k}(G,\mathbf{l},\mathbf{s})=\frac{1}{\binom{N}{k}}\sum_{\mathcal{F}_{0}\in\mathbb{F}_{k}}\Phi(G,\mathbf{l},\mathbf{s};\mathcal{F}_{0}). This is a finite average over the initial failure sets of size k k . Weighting the members of 𝔽 k \mathbb{F}_{k} equally evaluates expected survival under uniformly random initial failures; targeted removal calls for a worst-case rather than an average-case objective and lies outside our scope. To obtain a single robustness score across failure sizes, we aggregate the average survival fractions over a set of failure sizes 𝒦 ⊆ { 0 , … , N } \mathcal{K}\subseteq\{0,\dots,N\} : (7) AUC ⁡ ( G , 𝐥 , 𝐬 ) = ∑ k ∈ 𝒦 w k ​ J k ​ ( G , 𝐥 , 𝐬 ) , \mathrm{AUC}(G,\mathbf{l},\mathbf{s})=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}w_{k}J_{k}(G,\mathbf{l},\mathbf{s}), where w k ≥ 0 w_{k}\geq 0 and ∑ k ∈ 𝒦 w k = 1 \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}w_{k}=1 . The weights specify how much emphasis is placed on different failure sizes. Plotting J k J_{k} against the failure fraction p = k / N p=k/N traces the survival curve J ⁡ ( p ) J(p) (Figure 3 shows an example), and with uniform weights the objective is the discretized area under that curve, hence the name AUC. In our experiments we place uniform weight on failure fractions p ∈ [ 0 , 0.5 ] p\in[0,0.5] and zero weight outside this range. This range focuses the evaluation on low-to-moderate failure fractions, where robustness depends strongly on how the cascade propagates after the initial failures, while keeping the same evaluation criterion for all methods. In short, Φ \Phi is the basic survival metric for one cascade realization, J k J_{k} averages this metric over all initial failure sets of a given size, and AUC aggregates these across the evaluated failure sizes. Then, given an input graph G G and budget B B , the capacity allocation objective is (8) max 𝐬 ∈ Δ B ⁡ AUC ⁡ ( G , 𝐥 , 𝐬 ) . \max_{\mathbf{s}\in\Delta_{B}}\ \mathrm{AUC}(G,\mathbf{l},\mathbf{s}).

sections.heading: 2.2.3. Why the Optimization is Difficult
sections.text: Although the feasible set Δ B \Delta_{B} is simple, the objective in ( 8 ) is not. Each node’s survival is set by a hard overload threshold, so the outcome stays fixed as 𝐬 \mathbf{s} varies until a threshold is crossed, then jumps. The objective AUC ⁡ ( G , 𝐥 , 𝐬 ) \mathrm{AUC}(G,\mathbf{l},\mathbf{s}) is therefore step-like and non-concave: convex methods do not apply, and gradients are uninformative on flat regions and undefined at the jumps. Exact evaluation is also intractable: J k ​ ( G , 𝐥 , 𝐬 ) J_{k}(G,\mathbf{l},\mathbf{s}) sums over ( N k ) \binom{N}{k} initial failure sets, each requiring a full multi-round cascade. Because the outcome couples topology, load and capacity, and the location and order of failures, no closed-form characterization is available as in prior global-redistribution models ( Zhang and Yağan, 2016 ; Ozel et al., 2018 ; Irsoy and Yagan, 2026a ) , which motivates a simulation-based learning approach.

sections.heading: 3. Proposed TANGCO
sections.text: Figure 2. TANGCO turns a graph and its loads into a budget-feasible capacity allocation, trained end to end through the cascade simulator. Node features feed a message-passing policy whose residual output is projected onto the budget simplex; the simulator scores the resulting allocation, and the AUC reward drives a REINFORCE update. TANGCO combines a message-passing GNN policy with simulation-based reinforcement learning. For a fixed instance ( G , 𝐥 ) (G,\mathbf{l}) and free-space budget B B , the goal is to learn a policy that outputs an allocation 𝐬 ∈ Δ B \mathbf{s}\in\Delta_{B} with high robustness. Figure 2 summarizes the pipeline: node features feed a GNN policy, whose output is projected onto the budget simplex as a feasible free-space allocation. The allocation can only be evaluated through the cascade simulator, whose hard failure thresholds and discrete redistribution steps make the robustness score non-differentiable. We therefore train the policy with REINFORCE ( Williams, 1992 ) : at each iteration, the algorithm samples candidate allocations, scores them using empirical AUC rewards, and updates the policy from these rewards. The next subsections describe each component.

sections.heading: 3.1. Node Features and GNN Policy
sections.text: The allocation depends on both the load vector and each node’s local topology. We therefore use a message-passing GNN rather than learning N N unrelated parameters. The GNN shares parameters across nodes and aggregates multi-hop information, which is useful since failures can propagate beyond one round. For each node v v we compute a log-transformed feature vector 𝐱 v \mathbf{x}_{v} from its own load, its degree, the mean, maximum, and variance of its one-hop neighborhood loads, and its two-hop degree (Appendix A.3 gives the formulas). The GNN stacks K K message-passing layers; its architecture follows GraphSAGE ( Hamilton et al., 2017 ) with mean aggregation, differing in two respects: messages are normalized by the sender’s degree, in parallel with the load-redistribution mechanism where a failing node splits its load among its neighbors, and each layer adds a residual connection to its MLP update to avoid oversmoothing. A final linear map produces one scalar residual logit μ θ , v \mu_{\theta,v} per node, and we write 𝝁 θ ​ ( G , 𝐗 ) = ( μ θ , v ) v ∈ 𝒱 \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\theta}(G,\mathbf{X})=(\mu_{\theta,v})_{v\in\mathcal{V}} for the vector of outputs (Appendix A.4 gives the full equations). The output layer is zero-initialized, so the initial residual logits are exactly zero and the policy starts at the anchor allocation described next.

sections.heading: 3.2. Residual Softmax Allocation
sections.text: Directly searching over all allocations in Δ B \Delta_{B} is high-dimensional and noisy. We therefore learn a residual correction around a fixed anchor allocation: the anchor gives the policy a reasonable starting point, and the GNN shifts capacity from it using the graph and load features. Let 𝐬 anchor ∈ Δ B \mathbf{s}^{\mathrm{anchor}}\in\Delta_{B} be a fixed anchor allocation. We use two anchors in the experiments. The first is the uniform allocation, (9) s v uniform = B N . s_{v}^{\mathrm{uniform}}=\frac{B}{N}. Beyond serving as an intuitive baseline, the uniform allocation is optimal under global redistribution, where the network is treated as fully connected ( Zhang and Yağan, 2016 ) , with extensions to partial load loss ( Ozel et al., 2018 ) and max-load targeted attacks ( Ozel et al., 2019 ) . The second anchor is a local-redistribution heuristic. Irsoy and Yağan ( Irsoy and Yagan, 2026b ) allocate free space in proportion to a node’s one-hop local-risk, giving the Localized Risk-based Free-Space Allocation (LR-FSA) heuristic, (10) s v lrfsa = B ​ r v ∑ u ∈ 𝒱 r u , r v = ∑ u ∈ 𝒩 ⁡ ( v ) ℓ u d u . s_{v}^{\mathrm{lrfsa}}=B\frac{r_{v}}{\sum_{u\in\mathcal{V}}r_{u}},\qquad r_{v}=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}\frac{\ell_{u}}{d_{u}}. The score r v r_{v} estimates the load that node v v may receive from its neighbors in one round of local redistribution. We train a separate policy for each anchor. Reported TANGCO performance uses the better of the two completed runs (each trained and evaluated independently), a two-start procedure that uses the cascade simulator already required for training. During training, the GNN output 𝝁 θ ​ ( G , 𝐗 ) \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\theta}(G,\mathbf{X}) is treated as the mean of a Gaussian over residual logits. We sample residual logits as (12) 𝐳 ( b ) ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝝁 θ ​ ( G , 𝐗 ) , σ 2 ​ I ) , \mathbf{z}^{(b)}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\theta}(G,\mathbf{X}),\sigma^{2}I\right), where σ > 0 \sigma>0 controls exploration and is annealed downward over training, and add the residual to the anchor logits before a softmax that projects onto the budget simplex: (13) s v ( b ) = B ​ exp ⁡ ( a v anchor + z v ( b ) ) ∑ u ∈ 𝒱 exp ⁡ ( a u anchor + z u ( b ) ) , v ∈ 𝒱 . s_{v}^{(b)}=B\frac{\exp\left(a_{v}^{\mathrm{anchor}}+z_{v}^{(b)}\right)}{\sum_{u\in\mathcal{V}}\exp\left(a_{u}^{\mathrm{anchor}}+z_{u}^{(b)}\right)},\qquad v\in\mathcal{V}. By construction, 𝐬 ( b ) ∈ Δ B \mathbf{s}^{(b)}\in\Delta_{B} for every sample. At initialization 𝝁 θ = 0 \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\theta}=0 (Section 3.1 ), so the deterministic policy with σ = 0 \sigma=0 exactly recovers the anchor, while stochastic samples are centered around it in logit space; as training progresses the GNN learns residual adjustments that improve robustness. The residual parameterization gives REINFORCE a warm start and reduces training noise, at the cost of restricting the search to softmax perturbations of the chosen anchor. This is not binding in our experiments, where the best allocation builds on one of the two anchors in every tested case, but it motivates future work on improved anchors and less anchor-tied parameterizations.

sections.heading: 3.3. Simulator-Based Reward
sections.text: Each sampled allocation is scored by the cascade model of Section 2.1 . Exact AUC evaluation is infeasible, so we use a Monte Carlo estimate: over a finite grid 𝒫 \mathcal{P} of failure fractions, we draw M M initial failure sets ℱ p , 1 , … , ℱ p , M \mathcal{F}_{p,1},\dots,\mathcal{F}_{p,M} of size ⌊ p ​ N ⌋ \lfloor pN\rfloor at each p ∈ 𝒫 p\in\mathcal{P} , giving the empirical survival fraction (14) J ^ p ​ ( G , 𝐥 , 𝐬 ) = 1 M ​ ∑ m = 1 M Φ ⁡ ( G , 𝐥 , 𝐬 , ℱ p , m ) , \widehat{J}_{p}(G,\mathbf{l},\mathbf{s})=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\Phi(G,\mathbf{l},\mathbf{s};\mathcal{F}_{p,m}), and the reward is the empirical AUC over the grid, (15) R ⁡ ( 𝐬 ) = AUC ^ ​ ( G , 𝐥 , 𝐬 ) = 1 | 𝒫 | ​ ∑ p ∈ 𝒫 J ^ p ​ ( G , 𝐥 , 𝐬 ) , R(\mathbf{s})=\widehat{\mathrm{AUC}}(G,\mathbf{l},\mathbf{s})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\widehat{J}_{p}(G,\mathbf{l},\mathbf{s}), the empirical counterpart of ( 7 ) with uniform weights. Appendix A.5 details how the grid 𝒫 \mathcal{P} is chosen and how failure sets are pre-sampled and shared across allocations.

sections.heading: 3.4. Non-differentiable Optimization
sections.text: The cascade simulator contains threshold failures and discrete rounds, so we cannot differentiate through it. We instead maximize the expected empirical AUC under the stochastic residual-logit policy, (16) 𝒥 ⁡ ( θ ) = 𝔼 𝐳 ∼ p θ ​ [ AUC ^ ​ ( G , 𝐥 , 𝐬 ⁡ ( 𝐳 ) ) ] , \mathcal{J}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim p_{\theta}}\left[\widehat{\mathrm{AUC}}\left(G,\mathbf{l},\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{z})\right)\right], for a fixed instance ( G , 𝐥 ) (G,\mathbf{l}) , budget B B , and anchor, where p θ p_{\theta} is the Gaussian in ( 12 ) and 𝐬 ⁡ ( 𝐳 ) \mathbf{s}(\mathbf{z}) the softmax allocation in ( 13 ). We optimize it with REINFORCE: the score-function estimator turns the simulator’s scalar reward into a gradient on the GNN parameters through the log-probability of the sampled logits, and we reduce its variance with a batch-mean baseline over the Q Q samples per iteration and stabilize it with a small L2 penalty on the residual logits (Appendix A.5 ). We train with Adam ( Kingma and Ba, 2015 ) , periodically evaluate the deterministic policy ( σ = 0 \sigma=0 ) on a held-out set of failure samples, and keep the allocation with the best validation AUC as the final output for that instance.

sections.heading: 4. Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate TANGCO through the following research questions (RQs): • RQ1: Effectiveness Does TANGCO improve robustness over the baseline heuristics? • RQ2: Transferability Does a trained policy transfer to held-out instances within a family, and across families? • RQ3: Scalability How does TANGCO ’s allocation optimization grow with network size? • RQ4: Gain Attribution Does the gain come from message-passing inductive bias or black-box numerical optimization? • RQ5: Gain Characterization Which topologies, load distributions, and budgets yield the largest robustness gains? sections.heading: Graphs.
sections.text: We use five synthetic families and five real-world networks spanning power, road, air-transport, and Internet router/AS domains. Each synthetic family has N = 5000 N=5000 nodes and about 12 12 edges per node, and captures a distinct structural regime: ER (homogeneous degrees, no hubs), PowL (a heavy-tailed degree distribution, exponent γ = 2.5 \gamma=2.5 ), ClusPowL (the same degrees with local clustering C c ≈ 0.15 C_{c}\approx 0.15 ), CorPer (a dense core with a sparse periphery), and RandGeo (spatial proximity edges with high clustering). The five real networks span few infrastructure domains: the Western US power grid ( N = 4941 N=4941 ), the Oregon AS graph ( N = 10,670 N=10{,}670 ), the Chicago road network ( N = 12,979 N=12{,}979 ), the OpenFlights airport network ( N = 3188 N=3188 ), and the Rocketfuel AS1221 topology ( N = 3515 N=3515 ). They cover a diverse set of structures, from near-planar (Chicago, maximum degree 7 7 ) to hub-heavy (OpenFlights and Oregon, maximum degree 248 248 and 2312 2312 ). Appendix A.2 gives generation procedures, citations, and per-graph statistics. For each synthetic family we generate ten independent realizations and report the mean over the ten.

sections.heading: Loads and budgets.
sections.text: We evaluate each graph under three initial-load distributions: uniform (bounded variation around the mean), Pareto (a heavy tail, so a few nodes carry much larger loads), and bimodal (a two-group high/low mixture). The budget B B is the total free space to allocate; we set B / ∑ v ℓ v ∈ { 0.5 , 0.75 , 1.0 } B/\sum_{v}\ell_{v}\in\{0.5,0.75,1.0\} , from tight to loose, giving nine load-budget conditions in all.

sections.heading: Baseline heuristics.
sections.text: We compare TANGCO with four deterministic capacity rules from the cascade literature, all normalized to ∑ v s v = B \sum_{v}s_{v}=B : the two anchors of Section 3.2 , Uniform (equal free space) and LR-FSA (one-hop local-risk); Load , proportional to initial load ( Motter and Lai, 2002 ) ; and Degree , proportional to degree ( Li et al., 2008 ) . sections.heading: Architecture, training, and protocol.
sections.text: We use K = 3 K=3 message-passing layers and hidden width 64 64 throughout, except in the depth ablation of Section 4.5 , and train each instance with Adam ( Kingma and Ba, 2015 ) (Appendix A.5 lists all hyperparameters). We report the robustness score AUC ⁡ ( G , 𝐥 , 𝐬 ) \mathrm{AUC}(G,\mathbf{l},\mathbf{s}) of Eq. ( 7 ), the average survival fraction over p ∈ [ 0 , 0.5 ] p\in[0,0.5] . The primary comparison is TANGCO (maximum AUC over the two anchors) against the best heuristic (maximum AUC over Uniform , Degree , Load , LR-FSA ) on each configuration. We replicate training over five seeds per configuration and report the mean; training-seed variance is small (Appendix A.5 ).

sections.heading: 4.2. Overall Performance (RQ1)
sections.text: Figure 3 shows a robustness curve for a representative instance and makes the AUC metric concrete: each curve traces the survival fraction as the failure fraction grows, and a more robust allocation keeps the curve higher for longer, enclosing more area. TANGCO pushes its curve well to the right of every heuristic, holding a high survival fraction out to roughly twice the failure fraction that the heuristics withstand. Figure 4 compares the absolute AUC of the four heuristics and the two anchored policies at a representative configuration, uniform load and B = 0.75 B=0.75 . Table 1 reports the relative improvement of TANGCO over the best heuristic across all nine load-budget conditions. Two observations follow. • TANGCO improves on the best heuristic in almost every condition. Figure 4 shows the comparison on seven representative networks at uniform load and B = 0.75 B=0.75 , where TANGCO exceeds every heuristic. Table 1 extends it to the full set: the policy improves on the best heuristic in all 450 450 synthetic cells ( 5 5 families × \times 9 9 conditions × \times 10 10 realizations) and in 40 40 of the 45 45 real-world conditions, with gains from + 1.6 % +1.6\% on ER at a loose budget to + 246 % +246\% on OpenFlights . sections.heading: 4.3. Transferability (RQ2)
sections.text: Every result so far trains one policy per graph instance. We now ask whether a trained policy transfers to unseen graphs: first across held-out instances within and between families, then as a model deployable on any new network. Per-graph policies transfer within a family and across families that share structure. For within-family transfer we train one policy jointly on eight of a family’s ten realizations and evaluate it on the two held out; for cross-family transfer we apply each such policy to every other family’s held-out graphs. Table 2 reports the 5 × 5 5\times 5 source-to-target matrix of improvement in AUC over the best heuristic (uniform load, B = 0.75 B=0.75 ), with per-instance training in the bottom row. sections.heading: 4.5. Ablations: Optimizer and Depth (RQ4)
sections.text: A learned policy could beat heuristics by searching the allocation space more thoroughly than any fixed formula, or by encoding graph structure through message passing. We isolate the first with two variants that optimize a free allocation vector directly, No-GNN (same REINFORCE protocol as TANGCO ) and a derivative-free CMA-ES optimizer, and the second by varying message-passing depth (Appendix B.4 , B.5 ). Direct search stays near the best heuristic whether policy-gradient or evolutionary; message passing carries the gain. No-GNN barely clears the best heuristic (mean Δ \Delta AUC − 0.001 -0.001 uniform, + 0.002 +0.002 Pareto); CMA-ES gains more ( + 0.009 +0.009 , + 0.012 +0.012 ), mostly on hub-heavy graphs, reaching 0.145 0.145 on OpenFlights against a heuristic 0.076 0.076 , but still falls well short of TANGCO ( 0.262 0.262 ). Both lose on AS1221, where Degree is already strong. TANGCO beats the No-GNN variant in all 10 10 uniform cells (mean + 0.052 +0.052 AUC; Table 3 ) and in all 10 10 Pareto cells, and beats the CMA-ES variant in every cell (Appendix B.4 ). One message-passing hop is enough. sections.heading: 4.6. What Drives the Gains (RQ5)
sections.text: TANGCO ’s gains concentrate on heterogeneous topologies at intermediate budgets. Analyzing the learned allocations shows local risk is a strong signal in some regimes but incomplete in others, where TANGCO draws on additional structural and nonlinear signals. • Gains scale with structural heterogeneity and peak at intermediate budgets. The largest improvements fall on heavy-tailed and hub-heavy topologies ( ClusPowL + 89 % +89\% , PowL + 65 % +65\% , OpenFlights up to + 246 % +246\% , Oregon AS up to + 108 % +108\% ), while homogeneous ER stays between + 1.6 % +1.6\% and + 18.1 % +18.1\% . Across budgets the gain is largest where the baseline is weak but survivable: it shrinks with budget on the strong-baseline families and grows with budget on the weak-baseline ones. Chicago and the US grid are the extreme, with no gain at B = 0.5 B{=}0.5 until the budget buys enough survival to reallocate (Table 1 ). • A systematic, nested analysis identifies local risk as the primary signal the policy uses, and where it falls short. We fit the normalized allocation log ⁡ ( s v / ( B / N ) ) \log\!\left(s_{v}/(B/N)\right) with a nested model sequence: the one-hop local-risk score r v r_{v} (Eq. ( 10 )) alone, then cumulatively adding degree, load, and k k -core, then a generalized additive model where the linear fit fails (Appendix B.6 ). Local risk alone explains the allocation in regime A ( R 2 ≥ 0.90 R^{2}\geq 0.90 : the moderately heavy-tailed families PowL , ClusPowL , CorPer , and several networks under uniform load). The rest need either an additional local feature such as degree (regime B, e.g. RandGeo ) or nonlinear effects (regime C), as on the extreme-hub Oregon AS and AS1221, where a nonlinear fit reaches 0.82 0.82 – 0.98 0.98 against linear 0.03 0.03 – 0.33 0.33 . Local risk is thus strong but incomplete: TANGCO rescales capacity-versus-risk where it dominates and draws on higher-order structure elsewhere. • Tuned Local-Risk ( T-LR ) recovers most of the heuristic-to- TANGCO gap where local risk dominates. Regime A motivates fitting a per-graph exponent, s v ∝ r v γ s_{v}\propto r_{v}^{\gamma} , by a bounded search on training failures rather than fixing γ = 1 \gamma=1 . T-LR recovers about 85 % 85\% of the gap in regime A and matches TANGCO on OpenFlights ( 0.265 0.265 vs. 0.262 0.262 ; Table 4 ). Outside regime A it falls below the best heuristic on Oregon AS and AS1221, where only TANGCO ’s higher-order graph reasoning recovers the gain.

sections.heading: Cascading failures.
sections.text: Cascading failures in flow networks are a long-studied problem. The foundational model of Motter and Lai assigns each node a load equal to its betweenness and a capacity fixed to a multiple of that load; when a node fails its load redistributes to others, which may overload them and trigger a cascade ( Motter and Lai, 2002 ) . A large body of work builds on this setup to study how cascades propagate under different mechanisms, including interdependent networks where failures couple across systems ( Buldyrev et al., 2010 ) , dynamical recovery of failed nodes ( Majdandžić et al., 2014 ) , and heterogeneous rules for how a failed node’s load spreads to its neighbors ( Hou et al., 2017 ) . A related line engineers robustness by setting capacity as a fixed function of a local statistic, either a nonlinear function of load ( Wang and Kim, 2007 ) or a tuned power of node degree under a fixed budget ( Li et al., 2008 ) . These models treat capacity as a closed-form rule fit to load or degree, rather than an allocation optimized against the cascade itself. Fewer works take capacity allocation as a decision variable to optimize. Researchers optimize the capacity of a power system for robustness against cascades ( Zhang and Yağan, 2016 ) ; prove that a uniform redundancy allocation maximizes robustness under random failures and extend the analysis to max-load targeted attacks ( Ozel et al., 2018 ; Ozel et al., 2019 ) ; and derive optimal load-capacity allocations in multiplex networks ( Irsoy and Yagan, 2026a ) . These analyses assume global redistribution, where a failed node’s load spreads equally to all surviving nodes. Global redistribution yields clean, often closed-form optima, but it discards the network topology, and the resulting allocations do not transfer to local redistribution, where a node sheds load onto its neighbors and cascade outcomes depend on multi-round structure. Our baselines draw on both lines: the Uniform allocation follows the global-redistribution optimum ( Ozel et al., 2018 ; Zhang and Yağan, 2016 ; Irsoy and Yagan, 2026a ) , LR-FSA is a one-hop local-risk heuristic ( Irsoy and Yagan, 2026b ) , Degree instantiates the degree-weighted rule ( Li et al., 2008 ) , and Load the fixed-tolerance rule ( Motter and Lai, 2002 ) . Learning for graph problems. A separate line learns to solve graph optimization problems. Graph neural networks with reinforcement learning construct combinatorial solutions node by node ( Dai et al., 2017 ) , and learn constrained resource allocations such as wireless power control ( Eisen and Ribeiro, 2020 ) or resource distribution in observational science ( Cranmer et al., 2021 ) . These methods assume a differentiable objective or a differentiable relaxation ( Eisen and Ribeiro, 2020 ; Cranmer et al., 2021 ) . Our fail-or-survive cascade objective is piecewise-constant and non-differentiable, so we train TANGCO with score-function gradients (REINFORCE ( Williams, 1992 ) ) and keep the budget exact through a residual-softmax output. Learning for cascading failures. Closest to our setting is work that learns to predict or mitigate cascades. Like TANGCO , Mao et al. train a graph neural network with reinforcement learning against a cascade simulator, here to surface the most vulnerable nodes of interdependent urban infrastructure ( Mao et al., 2023 ) . Jhun et al. reinforce the highest-ranked nodes under a learned avalanche-centrality measure to suppress nonlocal cascades ( Jhun et al., 2023 ) ; others treat defense as an adversarial game over discrete targets ( Cunningham and Tucker, 2024 ) , steer spreading through node interventions ( Meirom et al., 2021 ) , or learn a diffusion surrogate ( Xiang et al., 2024 ) . A broader body predicts cascade outcomes and risk ( Bhaila and Wu, 2024 ; Zhu et al., 2023a ; Zhu et al., 2023b ) , identifies vulnerable node sets ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , and benchmarks these tasks ( Varbella et al., 2024 ) . All rank, classify, or discretely reinforce a node set; none outputs a continuous, budget-feasible capacity allocation optimized end-to-end through the overload cascade.

sections.heading: 6. Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced TANGCO , a topology-aware learning framework for capacity allocation under local load redistribution. The framework contributes in two ways. First, it provides a viable method for improving robustness when the cascade objective is non-differentiable and no analytical allocation rule is available. Second, it helps explain the allocation problem itself by identifying when local-risk is sufficient and when additional or nonlinear structure matters. This analysis led to Tuned Local-Risk ( T-LR ), a rule that improves on the original heuristic in the regimes it can represent, while also showing why a GNN remains necessary in regimes that cannot be reduced to a simple rule. TANGCO pre , pre-trained on synthetic graphs, transfers to unseen real networks at the deployment cost of a hand-designed heuristic, extending the method to settings without per-network training. TANGCO therefore serves both as an allocation method and as a tool for extracting simpler principles from cascade dynamics. Future work can extend the framework to domain-specific redistribution models and develop graph-adaptive anchor selection from features alone. Acknowledgements. sections.heading: A.2. Network Data
sections.text: We generate synthetic graphs in two settings that serve different purposes. The evaluation families fix one canonical setting per topology, so that any difference in results reflects structure alone. The curated training set does the opposite: it varies structure on purpose, so that a single pre-trained policy meets many regimes before it ever sees a test graph. Table 6 summarizes all three groups.

sections.heading: Synthetic evaluation families.
sections.text: All five families share N = 5000 N=5000 nodes and mean degree ⟨ k ⟩ ≈ 12 \langle k\rangle\approx 12 , and each fixes the one parameter that defines it. ER ( Erdős and Rényi, 1960 ; Newman, 2018a ) connects each pair of nodes independently with equal probability, giving even degrees and no pronounced hubs. PowL ( Newman et al., 2001 ; Newman, 2018b ) draws a power-law degree sequence (exponent γ = 2.5 \gamma=2.5 ) and wires it with the configuration model, so a few nodes act as strong hubs, as in communication, social, and information networks. ClusPowL ( Newman, 2009 ) keeps the PowL degree sequence but rewires it to raise the average local clustering to C ≈ 0.15 C\approx 0.15 , adding short cycles and redundant local paths; comparing it with PowL isolates the effect of clustering on cascade propagation. CorPer ( Borgatti and Everett, 2000 ) is a degree-corrected core–periphery model with a core fraction of 0.2 0.2 : a dense core carries the main cascade pathways and a sparse periphery surrounds it. RandGeo ( Dall and Christensen, 2002 ) places nodes in the unit square and joins those within a fixed radius, giving spatial locality, high clustering, and long paths, as in physically constrained networks such as road and grid systems.

sections.heading: Real-world networks.
sections.text: The five measured networks test whether the synthetic trends carry over to empirical topologies: the Western US power grid ( Rossi and Ahmed, 2015 ; Watts and Strogatz, 1998 ) , the Oregon AS graph ( Leskovec et al., 2005 ; Stanford Network Analysis Project, ) , the Chicago road network ( Peixoto, 2020 ) , the OpenFlights airport route network ( Opsahl et al., 2010 ; Peixoto, 2020 ) , and the Rocketfuel AS1221 router topology ( Spring et al., 2004 ) . Together they span the structural range of the synthetic families, from the low-degree, long-path grid and road networks to the extreme-hub AS and airport graphs (Table 6 ). OpenFlights carries a domain caveat: equal-split local redistribution is a stylized abstraction for air transport, since a substitutable airport is not always a route neighbor.

sections.heading: Curated training set.
sections.text: The pre-trained policy TANGCO pre never sees the canonical settings above. We train it on a curated suite of 64 64 synthetic graphs built for structural variety alone: 16 16 graphs from each of four families ( ER , PowL , CorPer , RandGeo ), spread across four size bands (roughly 2,000 2{,}000 to 15,000 15{,}000 nodes) and four mean-degree bands (from sparse, ⟨ k ⟩ ≈ 2 \langle k\rangle\approx 2 , to dense, ⟨ k ⟩ ≈ 16 \langle k\rangle\approx 16 ). Within each family we also open up the defining parameter instead of pinning it: the power-law exponent ranges over γ ∈ [ 2.1 , 3.2 ] \gamma\in[2.1,3.2] , the core–periphery core fraction over [ 0.11 , 0.45 ] [0.11,0.45] , and the random-geometric radius over [ 0.011 , 0.034 ] [0.011,0.034] . ER has no shape parameter, so only its size and density vary. We leave ClusPowL out of training on purpose. It is a clustered cousin of PowL , and the heavy-tailed families already transfer well among themselves (Table 2 ), so adding it would tilt the four-family balance toward that regime. Holding it out instead tests whether the policy carries over to a related family it never trained on. A second, independently drawn set of 64 64 graphs serves as validation, and we select the checkpoint by validation AUC. Table 6. sections.heading: Load distributions.
sections.text: The uniform loads are drawn from a bounded uniform distribution around the target mean, giving moderate variation without a heavy tail or distinct groups. The Pareto loads are drawn from a heavy-tailed distribution scaled so its expectation equals the target mean, so a small number of nodes carry much larger loads than the rest. The bimodal loads are drawn from a two-group mixture with a smaller high-load group and a larger low-load group, a structured heterogeneity distinct from the gradual Pareto tail.

sections.heading: A.3. Node Features
sections.text: The policy sees each node through a six-dimensional feature vector 𝐱 v \mathbf{x}_{v} that summarizes the node and its one-hop neighborhood, the locality the cascade redistributes over. For a node v v with load ℓ v \ell_{v} , degree d v = | 𝒩 ⁡ ( v ) | d_{v}=|\mathcal{N}(v)| , and neighborhood 𝒩 ⁡ ( v ) \mathcal{N}(v) , the entries are the log-transformed own load log ⁡ ( ℓ v + ϵ ) \log(\ell_{v}{+}\epsilon) , degree log ⁡ ( d v + 1 ) \log(d_{v}{+}1) , mean neighbor load log ⁡ ( ℓ ¯ v + ϵ ) \log(\bar{\ell}_{v}{+}\epsilon) , maximum neighbor load log ⁡ ( ℓ v max + ϵ ) \log(\ell^{\max}_{v}{+}\epsilon) , neighbor-load variance log ⁡ ( Var v + 1 ) \log(\mathrm{Var}_{v}{+}1) , and two-hop degree log ⁡ ( d v ( 2 ) + 1 ) \log(d^{(2)}_{v}{+}1) , where ℓ ¯ v = 1 d v ​ ∑ u ∈ 𝒩 ⁡ ( v ) ℓ u , ℓ v max = max u ∈ 𝒩 ⁡ ( v ) ⁡ ℓ u , Var v = 1 d v ​ ∑ u ∈ 𝒩 ⁡ ( v ) ( ℓ u − ℓ ¯ v ) 2 , \bar{\ell}_{v}=\tfrac{1}{d_{v}}\!\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}\!\ell_{u},\quad\ell^{\max}_{v}=\!\max_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}\!\ell_{u},\quad\mathrm{Var}_{v}=\tfrac{1}{d_{v}}\!\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}\!(\ell_{u}-\bar{\ell}_{v})^{2}, and d v ( 2 ) = ∑ u ∈ 𝒩 ⁡ ( v ) d u d^{(2)}_{v}=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}d_{u} is the summed degree of v v ’s neighbors. The log transform compresses the heavy-tailed loads and degrees into a comparable range, with ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon=10^{-8} keeping it finite at zero; isolated nodes take the four neighborhood features as zero before the log. The mean and maximum neighbor loads capture the two ways a node is stressed under local redistribution, a steady inflow from many neighbors or a spike from one failing hub, and the two-hop degree signals how far a local failure can spread in a second round.

sections.heading: A.4. GNN Architecture
sections.text: The policy is a message-passing GNN in the GraphSAGE family ( Hamilton et al., 2017 ) , with degree-normalized mean aggregation ( Kipf and Welling, 2017 ) and a residual update at each layer. It first maps each feature vector to a hidden state, (17) 𝐡 v ( 0 ) = ψ in ​ ( 𝐱 v ) , \mathbf{h}_{v}^{(0)}=\psi_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathbf{x}_{v}), with ψ in \psi_{\mathrm{in}} a linear map into width h h . At layer i i , each node collects messages from its neighbors, normalized by the sender’s degree so that it parallels the load redistribution logic in the cascade, (18) 𝐦 u → v ( i ) \displaystyle\mathbf{m}_{u\to v}^{(i)} = 𝐡 u ( i ) max ⁡ { d u , 1 } , \displaystyle=\frac{\mathbf{h}_{u}^{(i)}}{\max\{d_{u},1\}}, (19) 𝐚 v ( i ) \displaystyle\mathbf{a}_{v}^{(i)} = ∑ u ∈ 𝒩 ⁡ ( v ) 𝐦 u → v ( i ) , \displaystyle=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}\mathbf{m}_{u\to v}^{(i)}, and updates its state with an MLP on the concatenation of the current state and the aggregate, wrapped in a residual connection, (20) 𝐡 v ( i + 1 ) = MLP i ( 𝐡 v ( i ) ∥ 𝐚 v ( i ) ) + 𝐡 v ( i ) , \mathbf{h}_{v}^{(i+1)}=\mathrm{MLP}_{i}\!\left(\mathbf{h}_{v}^{(i)}\,\|\,\mathbf{a}_{v}^{(i)}\right)+\mathbf{h}_{v}^{(i)}, where ∥ \| is concatenation. The residual connection lets the network add depth without the oversmoothing that would otherwise pull neighboring node states together as layers stack. After K K layers a linear head reads out one scalar residual logit per node, (21) μ θ , v = ψ out ​ ( 𝐡 v ( K ) ) , \mu_{\theta,v}=\psi_{\mathrm{out}}\!\left(\mathbf{h}_{v}^{(K)}\right), collected into 𝝁 θ ​ ( G , 𝐗 ) = ( μ θ , v ) v ∈ 𝒱 \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\theta}(G,\mathbf{X})=(\mu_{\theta,v})_{v\in\mathcal{V}} , where θ \theta gathers all layer parameters. The head ψ out \psi_{\mathrm{out}} is zero-initialized, so every residual logit starts at zero and the policy begins training exactly at the anchor allocation of Section 3.2 .

sections.heading: Policy gradient.
sections.text: We optimize the objective ( 16 ) with REINFOR-CE ( Williams, 1992 ) . The score-function identity gives (22) ∇ θ 𝒥 ​ ( θ ) = 𝔼 𝐳 ∼ p θ ​ [ AUC ^ ​ ( G , 𝐥 , 𝐬 ⁡ ( 𝐳 ) ) ​ ∇ θ ​ log ⁡ p θ ​ ( 𝐳 ∣ G , 𝐗 ) ] , \nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{J}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim p_{\theta}}\left[\widehat{\mathrm{AUC}}\left(G,\mathbf{l},\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{z})\right)\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}\mid G,\mathbf{X})\right], so the simulator enters only through the scalar reward, and the gradient flows through the log-probability of the sampled residual logits, which is differentiable in θ \theta . At each iteration we sample Q Q residual-logit vectors 𝐳 ( 1 ) , … , 𝐳 ( Q ) \mathbf{z}^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{z}^{(Q)} , each yielding an allocation 𝐬 ( b ) \mathbf{s}^{(b)} and reward R ( b ) = AUC ^ ​ ( G , 𝐥 , 𝐬 ( b ) ) R^{(b)}=\widehat{\mathrm{AUC}}(G,\mathbf{l},\mathbf{s}^{(b)}) , and subtract the batch mean as a baseline, (23) A ( b ) = R ( b ) − R ¯ , R ¯ = 1 Q ​ ∑ b = 1 Q R ( b ) . A^{(b)}=R^{(b)}-\bar{R},\qquad\bar{R}=\frac{1}{Q}\sum_{b=1}^{Q}R^{(b)}. The training loss combines the baselined policy-gradient term with a small L2 penalty on the residual logits, (24) ℒ RL ( θ ) = − 1 Q ∑ b = 1 Q A ( b ) log p θ ( 𝐳 ( b ) ∣ G , 𝐗 ) + λ N ‖ 𝝁 θ ( G , 𝐗 ) ‖ 2 2 , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RL}}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{Q}\sum_{b=1}^{Q}A^{(b)}\log p_{\theta}\left(\mathbf{z}^{(b)}\mid G,\mathbf{X}\right)+\frac{\lambda}{N}\left\|\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\theta}(G,\mathbf{X})\right\|_{2}^{2}, where the penalty keeps the residual logits from drifting far from the anchor and stabilizes the policy-gradient updates.

sections.heading: Hyperparameters.
sections.text: The policy uses K = 3 K=3 message-passing layers of hidden width 64 64 , each update a two-layer ReLU MLP with a residual connection, and a zero-initialized linear readout. We train each instance with Adam ( Kingma and Ba, 2015 ) at learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} for 200 200 iterations, drawing Q = 32 Q=32 sampled allocations per iteration and annealing the exploration scale σ \sigma linearly from 0.3 0.3 to 0.1 0.1 , with an L2 penalty λ = 10 − 4 \lambda=10^{-4} on the residual logits. Training rewards use 32 32 failure samples per failure fraction on a 41 41 -point grid covering the informative band of the anchor’s survival curve; reported AUC uses 100 100 samples on a fixed 101 101 -point grid over p ∈ [ 0 , 0.5 ] p\in[0,0.5] . We draw the evaluation failure sets independently of the training sets and fix them across all methods, so reported AUC scores every allocation on the same unseen failures. We replicate training over five seeds per configuration (realization, load, budget, anchor) and report AUC averaged over the five; the per-cell standard deviation in TANGCO AUC is ≈ 0.001 \approx 0.001 – 0.010 0.010 .

sections.heading: B.2. Transferability
sections.text: This appendix details the two transfer settings of Section 4.3 and reports the full per-target results. In the per-graph setting, each family contributes ten independent realizations. We train one policy jointly on eight of them for 400 400 iterations and evaluate it on the two held out, which forms the within-family diagonal of Table 2 . For the cross-family entries, we take each per-family policy and apply it, without retraining, to the held-out graphs of every other family. Tables 7 and 8 report every policy, including TANGCO pre , as absolute AUC under both loads. TANGCO pre is pre-trained on the curated suite of 64 64 synthetic graphs described in Appendix A.2 , and sees no real network or test graph during training. The test targets are never seen in training: the held-out realizations of the five evaluation families and the five real networks. Because one policy must fit many graphs at once, pre-training runs longer than per-instance training, 6,400 6{,}400 iterations against 200 200 ; all other settings match Appendix A.5 . Under Pareto load the transfer picture matches uniform load. Within-family transfer stays positive on all five families and lands within 0.001 0.001 AUC of per-instance training on four of them. Cross-family transfer improves on the target heuristic in 14 14 of 20 20 cells, against 17 17 under uniform load. The six failures are the pairs whose structure differs most: a random-geometric policy applied to the heavy-tailed families, an ER policy applied to the heavy-tailed and spatial families, and a core-periphery policy applied to RandGeo . RandGeo is the one family whose diagonal moves between loads: a shared within-family policy exceeds per-instance training by 0.010 0.010 AUC under uniform load, while per-instance training is ahead by the same margin under Pareto load. sections.heading: B.3. Scalability Details
sections.text: The policy adds one forward and one backward pass per training iteration, each O ⁡ ( K ⁡ ( E ​ h + N ​ h 2 ) ) O\!\left(K(Eh+Nh^{2})\right) for K K message-passing layers of width h h : message passing contributes O ⁡ ( E ​ h ) O(Eh) and the per-node update O ⁡ ( N ​ h 2 ) O(Nh^{2}) per layer. At the settings of Section 4.1 ( K = 3 K=3 , h = 64 h=64 ) this is negligible beside the ≈ 8.4 \approx 8.4 M cascade simulations per run, each O ⁡ ( N ​ t ¯ + E ) O(N\bar{t}+E) , as Figure 1 (c) confirms. At every network size the cascade simulator accounts for over 94 % 94\% of the training time and the GNN forward and backward passes for under 2 % 2\% . A full 200 200 -iteration run takes 24 24 to 50 50 minutes at 40,000 40{,}000 nodes on 16 16 CPU cores, and under nine minutes on every evaluated network. The cascade simulations are independent, and the implementation exploits this: the M M failure sets at a given allocation and failure fraction are simulated in parallel. The Q Q sampled allocations and the | 𝒫 | |\mathcal{P}| failure fractions are likewise independent and are currently evaluated in sequence, so further parallelism is available without changing the method. Figure 7 extends the deployment comparison to both load distributions. Figure 6 redraws the size-scaling result against edge count. The synthetic families hold mean degree fixed, so their edge count is proportional to node count and the three curves keep their near-linear slopes. The real networks separate by cascade depth. Sparse networks such as US grid and AS1221 sit above the trend: their longer cascades inflate the O ⁡ ( N ​ t ¯ ) O(N\bar{t}) term that dominates each simulation (Section 2.1 ). Edge count alone underpredicts their cost, which confirms that the node-sweep term drives runtime.

sections.heading: B.4. No-GNN Ablation
sections.text: The No-GNN variant tests whether reward-driven search alone can match TANGCO without message passing. It replaces the GNN by a free residual logit Δ ​ μ v \Delta\mu_{v} per node, zero-initialized so that the deterministic allocation matches the training anchor at the start of training, and feeds that residual into the same residual-softmax allocation head as TANGCO (Section 3.2 ). Training uses the same REINFORCE loop, Adam schedule, exploration annealing, L2 penalty on residual logits, failure-sample counts, two anchors ( Uniform , LR-FSA ), five seeds, and 200 200 iterations as the instance- TANGCO runs. The ablation covers all ten networks (five synthetic families and five reals); one realization represents each family, and both learned policies are five-seed means. We report the better of the two anchors, taking the best-validation-AUC checkpoint per seed as in the primary protocol (Section 3.4 ). Table 9 collects the uniform and Pareto results at B = 0.75 B=0.75 ; the body Table 3 shows the uniform block alone. TANGCO beats the No-GNN variant in all 20 20 cells (mean + 0.052 +0.052 AUC under uniform load, + 0.050 +0.050 under Pareto). Message passing matters most on the hub-heavy real networks: on OpenFlights the No-GNN variant barely clears the heuristic ( 0.083 0.083 vs. 0.076 0.076 ) while TANGCO more than triples it ( 0.262 0.262 ). On AS1221 the Degree heuristic ( 0.263 0.263 ) outranks both search variants, which improve only modestly on the shared Uniform anchor ( 0.213 0.213 and 0.235 0.235 from 0.205 0.205 ); TANGCO moves further to 0.286 0.286 and alone surpasses it. Many networked systems, from power grids to traffic networks and cloud clusters, carry loads across nodes with limited capacity. A node whose load exceeds its capacity fails and sheds its load onto its neighbors, which can trigger a system-wide cascade. We study how to allocate a fixed capacity budget across nodes to resist these cascades under local load redistribution. The problem is difficult because no optimal allocation is known, and the fail-or-survive objective is non-differentiable and piecewise constant, so exact and gradient-based optimization methods do not directly apply. We introduce TANGCO (Topology-Aware Neural Graph-Guided Capacity Optimization), which uses a graph neural network policy trained through the cascade simulator with policy-gradient learning and a heuristic anchor. We evaluate TANGCO on five synthetic graph families and five real networks spanning power, road, air, and Internet topologies. The learned policy improves on the best of four hand-designed heuristics in all 450 synthetic instances and in 40 of 45 real-network conditions, with robustness gains ranging from 1.6% to 246%. The learned policies transfer to unseen graphs within a family and partially across related topologies, and TANGCO pre , pre-trained on synthetic graphs, matches per-network training on unseen real networks. Training scales near-linearly with graph size, and TANGCO pre allocates on a new network with no per-target training, matching the deployment cost of a hand-designed heuristic. Free-vector variants without the GNN, trained by policy gradient or by CMA-ES, stay close to the heuristics, so the graph representation carries the gain beyond numerical search; the depth analysis shows most of it arises from one-hop information. Finally, analysis of the learned allocations identifies when local risk is sufficient, leads to an improved closed-form heuristic, and reveals the regimes where a topology-aware learned policy remains necessary. Keywords: cascading failures, capacity allocation, graph neural networks, reinforcement learning 1. Introduction Modern online services run on clusters of servers that share a request load. When one server becomes overloaded, its share of the load shifts to the remaining servers; if their updated load with the addition exceeds their capacity, they fail in turn, triggering a cascade that can end in a system-wide collapse. Such overload-driven cascades are a well-documented cause of large-scale outages at major cloud providers ( Bronson et al., 2021 ) . The same pattern is prevalent across many networked systems, including power grids ( Andersson et al., 2005 ) , transportation and traffic networks ( Li et al., 2015 ; Ma et al., 2020 ) , supply chains ( Yang et al., 2021 ; Hao et al., 2023 ) , as well as financial systems where the failure of one institution imposes losses on its counterparties and can push them into failure ( Gai and Kapadia, 2010 ) . In each case a node carries a load and fails when that load exceeds its capacity, and a failed node passes its load to other functioning nodes. The failure of a few components can therefore propagate through the network and bring down the system ( Buldyrev et al., 2010 ) . Cascading failures are due to network effects, where entities are connected through dependencies in a graph. The interaction between the graph topology and the capacity allocation of nodes therefore becomes critical in the cascade dynamics. Flow-based models of cascading failure originate with Motter and Lai ( Motter and Lai, 2002 ) , who take each node’s load to be its betweenness centrality and set its capacity to a fixed multiple of that load, c = ( 1 + α ) ​ l c=(1+\alpha)l . A large literature builds on this model to relate network structure to robustness and to add mechanisms such as dynamical recovery of failed nodes ( Majdandžić et al., 2014 ) and heterogeneous rules for how a failed node’s load spreads to its neighbors ( Hou et al., 2017 ) . Almost all work in this line fixes the allocated capacity in advance and studies the robustness that results ( Motter and Lai, 2002 ; Wang and Kim, 2007 ; Li et al., 2008 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) . The capacity allocation is thus an input to the model rather than a quantity to be designed. In this work, we treat capacity as a decision variable and address the problem of allocating a limited capacity budget across nodes to maximize robustness against cascading failures, a question that has received far less attention. The few works that study this allocation problem ( Zhang and Yağan, 2016 ; Ozel et al., 2018 ; Irsoy and Yagan, 2026a ) solve it under a global redistribution rule, where a failed node’s load is shared equally among all surviving nodes, irrespective of graph topology. That assumption yields a closed-form characterization of the final system size, and its allocations carry optimality guarantees while treating the network as fully connected and discarding topology. Under local redistribution, where loads pass only to immediate neighbors, cascade outcomes depend jointly on the topology and the initial load and capacity, and the global-redistribution guarantees no longer apply. Existing allocations for local redistribution are hand-designed heuristics rather than optimized methods. Hence, even though prior work has studied robustness extensively by analyzing and modifying network structure, the design question of how to allocate capacities on a given network and load remains far less explored. In contrast, we ask how to allocate a fixed capacity budget over a given network under local redistribution, where no optimal allocation is known. We introduce TANGCO (Topology-Aware Neural Graph-Guided Capacity Optimization), which employs a graph neural network (GNN) to learn capacity allocations directly from cascade dynamics. Given a graph and its initial loads, TANGCO outputs a capacity allocation that satisfies a fixed capacity budget. Our paper introduces four main contributions: • Topology-aware capacity optimization: We cast capacity allocation as a topology-aware policy-learning problem and propose TANGCO to maximize robustness against cascading failures. Hard overload thresholds make the cascade objective piecewise-constant; TANGCO trains a GNN allocation policy from simulator AUC rewards with score-function updates, without differentiating through the discrete failures. • Synthetic Pre-training and Transfer: We also introduce TANGCO pre , pretrained on diverse synthetic graph topologies and load distributions, and demonstrate strong transfer to unseen real-world networks (Figure 1 ). • Effectiveness, Scalability, Speed: Across five graph families, three load distributions, three capacity budgets, and five real-world networks, TANGCO consistently outperforms four competitive heuristics. Training scales linearly with graph size, while TANGCO pre needs no per-target training, yielding the best latency–performance trade-off (Figure 1 ). • Characterizing Gains: We show that message passing contributes consistently beyond direct numerical optimization, develop a one-hop rule that recovers most gains in specific regimes, and find that TANGCO ’s gains are largest on heterogeneous topologies at intermediate capacity budgets. Node features feed a message-passing policy whose residual output is projected onto the budget simplex; the simulator scores the resulting allocation, and the AUC reward drives a REINFORCE update. TANGCO combines a message-passing GNN policy with simulation-based reinforcement learning. For a fixed instance ( G , 𝐥 ) (G,\mathbf{l}) and free-space budget B B , the goal is to learn a policy that outputs an allocation 𝐬 ∈ Δ B \mathbf{s}\in\Delta_{B} with high robustness. Figure 2 summarizes the pipeline: node features feed a GNN policy, whose output is projected onto the budget simplex as a feasible free-space allocation. The allocation can only be evaluated through the cascade simulator, whose hard failure thresholds and discrete redistribution steps make the robustness score non-differentiable. We therefore train the policy with REINFORCE ( Williams, 1992 ) : at each iteration, the algorithm samples candidate allocations, scores them using empirical AUC rewards, and updates the policy from these rewards. We therefore use a message-passing GNN rather than learning N N unrelated parameters. The GNN shares parameters across nodes and aggregates multi-hop information, which is useful since failures can propagate beyond one round.
